theme: The tongue; pride; plans and the LORD’s purposes
readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 18:1-19:29. Notice the sayings about the power of the tongue, the LORD as a refuge, and how God’s purposes stand above human plans.
settingTheScene: Chapters 18 and 19 continue to gather sayings on speech, friendship, wealth and poverty, and discipline. Some of the best loved lines in the book are here, including the strong tower and the friend who sticks closer than a brother. The sayings are loosely organized but return to central themes of the book.
observation: “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (18:13).
“The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe” (18:10).
“The rich man’s wealth is his strong city, and like a high wall in his imagination” (18:11).
“Death and life are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruits” (18:21).
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD” (18:22).
“A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (18:24).
“Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed” (19:17).
“Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand” (19:21).
interpretation:
Two strongholds are set side by side in chapter 18. The name of the LORD is a strong tower, and the rich man’s wealth is a strong city “in his imagination.” The comparison is sharp. The rich man imagines himself secure, but his wall is only in his mind. The righteous man runs to the LORD and is actually safe. We all have something we run to when life is threatening: money, a plan, a person, a reputation. Proverbs asks whether that thing is a real tower or an imagined one.

The proverbs on speech continue. “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly.” Listening before speaking is a mark of wisdom. “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” The tongue is a powerful instrument. The one who uses it will taste the results, good or bad.

A significant saying about friendship appears at the end of chapter 18. “A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.” Quantity is not the measure of friendship. A single faithful friend is worth more than a crowd. Believers have always seen in this verse a picture of Christ.

Chapter 19 contains a strong statement on caring for the poor: “Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him.” Generosity to the poor is loaning to God himself. He takes it personally. It is one of the Bible’s most striking ideas: the poor man is God’s debtor, and God promises to repay.

The key theological statement of the chapter is verse 21: “Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand.” We make many plans. Some come to nothing. But God’s purpose cannot be overturned. This is a comfort to those who trust him, and a warning to those who plot against him. And verse 23: “The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied.”
connection: Jesus is the friend who sticks closer than a brother. He said, “No longer do I call you servants… but I have called you friends” (John 15:15). He is the strong tower, the refuge of the weary (Hebrews 6:18). Matthew 25:40 shows that kindness to the least is kindness to Christ. In Acts 4:28 the plans of men against Jesus served only “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.”
application:
Name your “strong tower.” Is it the LORD, or something imaginary?

Practice listening fully before answering in your next important conversation.

Give something to a person in need this week, and think of it as lending to the LORD.
prayerPrompts: Run into the strong tower of God’s name, and tell him why you need it.
Ask him to guard your tongue and teach you to listen.
Thank Jesus, the friend who sticks closer than a brother.
